Implements [§10.5 and §11.4 of the design](docs/design/74-external-review.md). Part of #74; depends on slice 4.

- Review a real out-of-band PR with `@swarm review` and merge it only on its `external_review_judged` verdict.

Implements [§7 and §8 of the design](docs/design/74-external-review.md). Part of #74; depends on slice 2.

issues.body:
Implements [§6 of the design](docs/design/74-external-review.md). Part of #74; depends on slice 1.

- Add a new `ingest` stage and role, claimed by the `claudecode` worker.
- Fetch `refs/pull/<n>/head` into `refs/swarm/external/<task_id>` in the named repository. Verify the fetched object equals the PR's `headRefOid`, and equals any operator-named SHA.
- Set the review range to `merge-base(baseRefOid, head)..head`.
- Report `{head_sha, base_ref_sha, merge_base, changed_files, pr_number, pr_url, author_signals}`; the controller applies `external_candidate_registered` with that as evidence.
- A PR that is missing or has moved is a **refusal**. GitHub or git being unreachable is an **environment defect**, which goes to `EXTERNAL_INGEST_BLOCKED` and is repairable (#78's rule).

Implements [§4 of the design](docs/design/74-external-review.md) (merged at 983e324). Part of #74.

- Add `external_review_judged`, which carries `judgment` (`satisfied` / `changes_requested` / `decision_required`) and `rationale` in its payload and always lands in `EXTERNAL_REVIEWED` (§4, §11.2).
- `EXTERNAL_REVIEWED` is terminal; `admin_cancelled` applies to the other `EXTERNAL_*` states through the existing generic rule.
- **Graph-walk test:** from every `EXTERNAL_*` state, `READY_INTEGRATION`, `INTEGRATING`, `INTEGRATION_*` and `COMPLETE` are unreachable. The test walks the transition graph rather than listing edges, and is mutation-tested by adding an edge that opens a path.
- External tasks never write `approved_candidate_sha`.

Controller only; nothing can enter these states yet. That comes in slice 2.

issues.title: Annotate a superseded attempt's PR, so a rejected attempt shown as Merged is explained
issues.body:
## What happens

Since #73 (#68 Option A), a retry is authored *on top of* the rejected candidate. When a later attempt is approved and integrated, every earlier attempt becomes an ancestor on `main`, and GitHub marks those attempts' pull requests **Merged**.

Observed on `T-CMD-33baf083e2`, 2026-09-24:

| PR | Attempt | Verdict | GitHub shows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #87 | a1 `adcb245` | **rejected** (seq 515) | Merged (merge = `adcb245`) |
| #88 | a2 `7442ad4` | approved (seq 522) | Merged (merge = `7c929b8`) |

`main`'s content equals the approved attempt, and the ledger records only `7442ad4` as approved. But a reader on GitHub sees a rejected attempt marked "Merged", with nothing explaining why.

## Decision (operator, 2026-09-24)

- **Keep the history.** Rejected attempts stay in `main`'s history as literal ancestors of the approved commit. Squashing is rejected: it would destroy the exact-SHA provenance the integrator relies on, break the two-parent merge rule that `check_merge_parents` and `check_tree_identical` enforce, and hide the real work history. This behaviour is to be **documented** as intended.
- **Annotate the superseded PRs.** When an attempt is superseded, its PR gets an automated comment, so "Merged" is never left unexplained.

## Scope

1. **On retry publication** (`publication.py`, where `ensure_pull_request` opens attempt N's PR): when the activation is a retry, meaning `retry_base.resolve` returned `source == "rejected_candidate"`, post a comment on the previous attempt's PR:

   > Superseded by attempt N (#<new PR>, `<sha>`). This attempt was rejected at review (ledger seq <n>); the retry is built on it, so it becomes an ancestor of whatever is eventually merged. If attempt N or a later one is integrated, GitHub will show this PR as Merged. That reflects the history, not an approval.

   Find the previous PR from the rejected candidate's branch (`task/<id>-a<N-1>`) and head SHA, and match both. Post nothing if exactly one PR does not match.
2. **Idempotent:** a redelivered or re-run publication must not post twice. Check for an existing comment carrying a marker such as `<!-- superseded-by: <sha> -->`.
3. **Never blocking:** if commenting fails, log it and carry on. Publication of the new candidate must not fail because an old PR could not be annotated.
4. **Document the intended history** in the README or the integrator docs: rejected attempts are ancestors on `main` by design (#68), and a "Merged" badge on a rejected attempt's PR means ancestry, not approval.

## Not in scope

- Rewriting or squashing the attempt chain.
- Closing superseded PRs automatically. They close themselves as Merged once a later attempt is integrated. Whether to close them earlier, on budget exhaustion or cancellation, is a separate question.
- Backfilling #84–#86 (already closed by hand) or #87 (a comment can be added by hand if wanted).

## Acceptance

- Tests with a fake `gh`:
  - a retry publication posts exactly one annotation on the prior attempt's PR, naming the new PR and SHA;
  - a first attempt posts none;
  - a redelivery posts none;
  - an ambiguous or missing prior PR posts none and doesn't fail;
  - a `gh` failure doesn't fail publication.
- Mutation-tested: the retry-only condition, the idempotency marker, and the non-blocking failure path.

issues.title: The swarm cannot review a change it did not author (authorless candidates, external PR ingestion)
issues.body:
The swarm cannot review a change it did not author. That is the structural reason #58 keeps recurring and the mechanism behind #60's measurement that 5 of 250 commits on `main` came through the pipeline.

## What is blocked today

A review activation requires the task to be in `READY_REVIEW`, and there are exactly two transitions into it (`controller/states.py`):

```
("AUTHORING",   "candidate_submitted"): READY_REVIEW  (AUTHOR authority)
("NEEDS_HUMAN", "return_to_review"):    READY_REVIEW  (ADMIN authority)
```

`return_to_review` is reachable only as an operator response to an existing escalation (`controller/api.py:219`), so it presupposes a task that already went through authoring. The admin CLI offers no way to record a candidate: `status, sweep, repair, capacity, create-task, ready, issue, show, events, retry, cancel`.

`admin issue <task> <agent> <host> review --expected-parent --expected-candidate --repo-location` accepts everything a reviewer needs and *looks* like the answer. It is refused by the state gate, because the task was never authored.

So a commit produced outside the pipeline — a hand-authored PR, a pair-programmed change, anything a person wrote — cannot be given to the reviewer. The only way to force it is to emit `candidate_submitted` claiming a worker authored it, which writes a false statement into the ledger. That is not an option: see the 2026-09-22 handoff §1 on the ledger meaning what it says.

## Why it matters

Every merge to `main` since 2026-09-15 has been approved by a manually relayed verdict with no review activation and no recorded judgment — `a3e9537`, `206fce8`, `74dfaef`, `40291d8`, and #73 when it lands. That is #58, and #58 cannot be closed while the only changes the pipeline can review are the ones it wrote.

It is also the thing standing between "the pipeline works" and "the pipeline does our work". The swarm's own development is the largest available source of real tasks, and none of it is reviewable by the swarm.

## What to investigate

1. **An authorless candidate.** A first-class way to register a candidate the pipeline did not author — commit, parent, branch, repository — that produces its own event kind rather than impersonating `candidate_submitted`. The distinction has to survive into the ledger: "a person wrote this and asked for review" and "the author produced this" are different facts, and a reader must be able to tell them apart afterwards.
2. **Where the state machine should accept it.** A new transition into `READY_REVIEW` under ADMIN or OPERATOR authority, or a parallel state for externally-sourced review. Whether such a task may proceed to integration, or must stop at a verdict, is the substantive design question — autonomous merge of a human's commit is a different risk than autonomous merge of the swarm's own.
3. **Ingestion from a pull request.** Resolving a PR number to its head SHA, base, and branch needs a worker with a checkout and `gh`; the controller has neither. The evidence has to land in the ledger, not in the worker's report alone.
4. **What a verdict on an external candidate means.** The reviewer currently judges a candidate against a contract the planner wrote. An external PR has no contract. Either one is synthesised at ingestion, or the review is explicitly contractless and the verdict says so.

## Not in scope

Reviewing arbitrary third-party code, or anything that reaches the network to fetch a candidate — that is #69, and deliberately separate.

## Related

- #58 — relayed verdicts leave no ledger evidence. This is the structural cause.
- #60 — swarm development bypasses the swarm. This is what makes it unavoidable.
- #64 / #69 — which repository a review happens in, and whether it may fetch.

## How it was found

2026-09-22, attempting to obtain an exact-SHA pipeline verdict on #73 (the #68 fix, authored out-of-band). The swarm was resumed and healthy; there was simply no supported path, and the unsupported one would have required fabricating authorship.

issues.title: Supervisor heartbeat write fails intermittently (WinError 5), risking a duplicate supervisor via ensure
issues.body:
## What happens

The supervisor intermittently fails to write its heartbeat, on Windows, with a rename denial:

```
2026-09-21T17:59:18-0600 WARNING supervisor: could not write the heartbeat: [WinError 5] Access is denied: 'C:\swarm-prod\agent-swarm\control\supervisor.tmp' -> 'C:\swarm-prod\agent-swarm\control\supervisor.heartbeat'
```

Five occurrences in `control/supervisor.log` between 2026-09-21T17:59 and 2026-09-22T08:49, from a single supervisor process (pid 53864, started 2026-09-21T17:03). Process uniqueness was verified at the time of writing: one supervisor, three workers, no duplicates. So this is not two supervisors fighting over the file.

The write is a temp-file-plus-rename. On Windows the rename fails with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` when another handle is open on the destination without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE` — a reader, an indexer, or a virus scanner touching `supervisor.heartbeat` in the instant the replace is attempted. `swarm_ctl.sh status` reads that file, and the scheduled `AgentSwarmSupervisor` task runs `ensure` every five minutes, which calls `supervisor.py --liveness`, which reads it too. The failures are hours apart, so it is an intermittent race rather than a persistent lock.

## Why it matters — the uniqueness hazard

Each occurrence has so far been transient: the next cycle writes successfully and `swarm_ctl.sh status` reports `heartbeat : fresh`. The hazard is what happens if one does not.

`ensure` decides liveness from the heartbeat:

```
if "$PYTHON" "$REPO/supervisor.py" --liveness >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ensure: a supervisor is running and heartbeating"
  exit 0
fi

echo "ensure: no live supervisor; starting one"
exec "$BASH" "$REPO/swarm_ctl.sh" start
```

A live, healthy supervisor whose heartbeat has merely gone stale is indistinguishable here from a dead one. If a write failure — or a run of them — outlasts the staleness window, the five-minute `ensure` starts a **second** supervisor beside the first. Two supervisors issuing activations against one controller is the failure mode the self-heal path exists to prevent, reached through the self-heal path itself.

The current transience is luck, not a guard. Nothing bounds how long the contending handle is held.

## Suggested direction

Not prescriptive, but the shape that seems right:

1. **Retry the rename** with a short backoff before reporting failure. A contending handle is typically released in milliseconds; a few retries would convert nearly every occurrence into a non-event.
2. **Escalate a sustained failure.** A single failed write is a warning; N consecutive failures mean the supervisor knows it is about to be judged dead while alive, and that should reach the room (see the visibility gap in the 2026-09-22 handoff §6 — failures outside a task lifecycle do not surface in chat at all).
3. **Consider whether liveness should be two-sided.** The heartbeat is the authority, deliberately, because a pid file cannot say what wrote it (#46). But `--liveness` already checks the process behind the heartbeat; a stale heartbeat whose *named pid is still alive and is a supervisor* might warrant refusing to start a second one rather than assuming death.

Point 3 is a design question, not a foregone conclusion — writing it down because the fix for 1 and 2 alone leaves the hazard theoretically open.

## How it was found

Reading `swarm_ctl.sh status` output while verifying deployment state for #70, on 2026-09-22. Not previously recorded in any handoff.

issues.title: Design: should a reviewer fetch a pinned candidate its named repository lacks?
issues.body:
Split out of #64, which deliberately implements precedence and fail-closed refusal only.

When the repository the controller named does not contain the pinned candidate, the reviewer refuses with `environment_defect` (#64). Fetching the commit instead would have made the first production acceptance run succeed with no operator involvement, because the author pushes the branch before review is issued. It is still a separate decision, because it gives a reviewer a capability it does not have today.

## What it would introduce

- **Remote trust.** The reviewer would obtain the object it is judging from somewhere other than the repository the controller named. The value of the current design is that the candidate is already present in a place the controller recorded; fetching replaces that with "a remote said this is the object".
- **Credentials.** A fetch may require authentication, which means a credential reaching the review path — and refusal messages that must never carry it.
- **Ref selection.** This is the subtle one. `git fetch <remote> <sha>` is not universally supported: unless `uploadpack.allowReachableSHA1InWant` is set, a bare SHA cannot be fetched and the object must be reachable from an advertised ref. Fetching the branch by name and trusting its tip is exactly the mistake `review_packet.build` already refuses to make — a branch names whatever its tip happens to be at the moment it is read, and the branch may have moved since the activation was issued.
- **Network failure.** A reviewer that fetches can now fail in ways unrelated to the change: timeout, DNS, rate limit. Each needs to be distinguishable from "the candidate is genuinely absent".
- **Object retention.** A fetched object lands in a repository the controller named but the worker does not own. Left behind it is litter; garbage collected it may vanish between packet construction and a later read.

## If it is implemented

1. Fetch into a **temporary namespaced ref** (`refs/swarm/review/<activation_id>`), never into a branch and never into `FETCH_HEAD` alone.
2. **Verify the resulting object equals the controller-pinned SHA** before anything is read from it. Never trust the branch tip by name.
3. Refuse, as today, if the object cannot be obtained — fetching is an additional way to satisfy the precondition, never a way to relax it.
4. Delete the temporary ref when the review ends, including on failure.
5. Distinguish "absent" from "could not reach the remote" in the recorded reason, since only one of those is repairable by pushing.

## Why not now

#64's precedence fix is sufficient to remove the temporary `REVIEW_REPO` override in production, which is the immediate goal. Fetching changes what a reviewer is allowed to reach, and that deserves its own argument rather than arriving as a fallback inside a bug fix.

Related: #64.

issues.title: Creating a task through the hub takes four rejected attempts to discover the required format
issues.body:
Creating a task through the hub took four rejected attempts before the ingress accepted a submission. Every rejection was correct, cheap and clearly worded — and none of the requirements was discoverable before submitting.

## What happened

Recorded during the first production acceptance run (`T-CMD-99a5880f3e`):

| # | Refusal |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `the title is longer than 200 characters` |
| 2 | `` `project:` is required `` |
| 3 | `the objective is missing: add it after a blank line` |
| 4 | `` `base:` must be a full 40-character commit SHA; the controller has no checkout and cannot resolve a branch name `` |

Four round trips to learn a five-line format. Nothing was spent — all four were refused at ingress before any model call, which is the design working. The cost is entirely in the operator's patience, and a first-time operator would plausibly stop around the third.

## Why it is not simply a documentation gap

`controller/ingress.py`'s own header documents the grammar as:

```
* `@swarm <title>` / `@all <title>` draft a task authored by the default author.
```

That is the whole of it. The implementation additionally requires `project:`, `base:` and `paths:` each on its own line, an objective after a blank line, and a base given as a full 40-character SHA. The documented grammar and the accepted grammar are different languages.

## The cheap fix

`@swarm help` (or the first refusal) printing the full template:

```
@swarm <title, under 200 characters>
project: <name from repos.json>
base: <full 40-character sha>
paths: <writable paths>
context: <read-only paths, optional>
proof: <baseline|branch_only|..., optional>

<objective>
```

## The real fix

The stated goal is that an operator gives the hub an ordinary instruction. Resolving these automatically is what would achieve it:

- **project** — infer from the mentioned paths when exactly one registered project contains them; refuse only when ambiguous.
- **base** — the controller cannot resolve a ref because it has no checkout, which is correct and should stay. But a worker can: resolving `main` to a SHA is the same shape of question as "is X an ancestor of Y", and the answer can be pinned into the draft before confirmation, where the operator sees it.
- **paths** — a draft could propose them from the objective and let confirmation be where they are corrected, rather than requiring them up front.

The confirmation step already exists and already shows the operator exactly what will be created. That is the natural place for inferred values to be reviewed — the current design asks the operator to supply what the system could propose, and then confirms it anyway.

## Evidence for why this matters

23 of 34 tasks in the ledger are cancelled. Re-reading them, most are triage rejections or deliberate test runs rather than failures — but the friction recorded here is the kind that stops a system being used rather than the kind that breaks it. The ledger has no events between 2026-09-15 and this run.

Related: #62 (documentation slices), #64 (the defect this run surfaced).

issues.title: Organize repository without changing runtime behavior
issues.body:
The repository has outgrown its flat layout. This tracks organizing it in independently reviewable slices, none of which may change runtime behaviour.

**Not to be mixed with #61.** Sequenced after the deployment isolation and the acceptance task.

## Verified current state

Measured at `206fce8`, not estimated:

- **37 tracked root entries**, including 22 Python modules and 4 shell/batch scripts. Worker, planning, integration, deployment and supervisor code all sit together.
- **The README is stale in a way that misleads.** Line 103 reads: *"**No integrator.** `READY_INTEGRATION` is where tasks stop. Nothing merges."* The integrator exists (`integrator.py`), the ledger holds 8 `integration_completed` events, and 5 of those candidates are ancestors of `main`. A reader is told the system cannot do the thing it demonstrably does.
- **No dependency manifest exists** — no `pyproject.toml`, no `setup.py`, no `requirements.txt`. The dependency list is duplicated twice in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (identical lines in both jobs) and three more times across `docs/DEPLOY_PHASE0_HUB.md` and `docs/DEPLOY_PHASE1_CONTROLLER.md`.
- **Tests are split by accident**: `hub/test_*.py` alongside `hub/hub.py`, everything else under `tests/`. CI runs them as two separate invocations for that reason.
- **`docs/` mixes four kinds of document**: current reference (`SWARM_PROTOCOL_v7.md`), historical MVP evidence (`MVP1`…`MVP8`), deployment runbooks, and `proposals/`.

## View-budget pressure, which is worse than it looks

`DEFAULT_FILE_VIEW` is 50,000 characters — the window an author is shown. A module past it cannot be handed to a worker as a task.

```
 60001  120.0%  plan.py                        (known, in KNOWN_TOO_LARGE)
 57785  115.6%  tests/test_supervisor.py       *** over the cap and UNGUARDED ***
 49850   99.7%  chatgpt_worker.py
 48739   97.5%  authored_change.py
 48194   96.4%  swarm_control.py
 47750   95.5%  controller/api.py
 47660   95.3%  plan_run.py
 46126   92.3%  supervisor.py
 45477   91.0%  hub/test_integration_routes.py
 45127   90.3%  claude_worker.py
```

`tests/test_supervisor.py` is **already over the limit and nothing reports it**: `test_every_other_root_module_fits` globs `REPO_ROOT.glob("*.py")`, so only root modules are checked. Any task scoped to change the supervisor together with its tests — the pairing the contract discipline requires — cannot be authored today, and the budget test does not say so.

`chatgpt_worker.py` has ~150 characters of headroom. That is the same cliff `controller/activations.py` hit, which forced the split in #61.

## The constraint that makes slice 5 harder than it looks

`deploy_controller.sh` builds its file set as `FILES=(hub/hub.py)` plus `controller/*.py` — 13 files — computes a **build id** as a digest over exactly those, ships them to a fixed remote layout (`$APP/controller/`), and `preflight.py` refuses to start a worker unless the controller's running build, its on-disk build, and the checkout's computed build all agree.

Moving `controller/` under a package therefore breaks four things at once: the deploy file list, the remote layout, the build-id computation, and the preflight comparison — which is the mechanism that proves a deployment is genuine. Slice 5 must change the deploy script in the same PR and will produce a one-time build-id discontinuity that has to be expected rather than discovered.

Production also resolves paths from the repository root: `supervisor.py` uses its own location as the checkout, `swarm_control.CONTROL_DIR` derives from it, and the `AgentSwarmSupervisor` scheduled task names `/c/swarm-prod/agent-swarm/swarm_ctl.sh` literally.

## Slices

| PR | Scope | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Documentation inventory, README correction, `docs/` index. **Docs only** — no imports, runtime paths or production commands change | Low |
| 2 | Separate current docs from historical evidence and proposals | Low |
| 3 | Centralize dependencies and development commands | Medium |
| 4 | Move hub tests into `tests/hub/`, split CI jobs, and extend the view-budget guard beyond root modules | Medium |
| 5 | Packages for workers, planning, integration and runtime control, keeping stable root entrypoint wrappers; deploy script and build id updated in the same change | High |
| 6 | Remove compatibility wrappers, only once deployment and rollback tooling no longer relies on them | High |

Target shape:

```text
agent_swarm/{controller,workers,planning,integration,runtime}/
hub/  scripts/  tests/{controller,workers,hub,integration}/
docs/{architecture,operations,protocol,history}/
pyproject.toml  README.md  + stable root launchers
```

`swarm_ctl.sh`, `worker_ctl.sh` and `deploy_controller.sh` stay at the root throughout, so the scheduled task, the production checkout, the deployment commands and operator habits keep working.

## Suggested addition to slice 4

Extend `test_every_other_root_module_fits` to cover `tests/`, `hub/` and any package directories. The guard exists to make an unauthorable module fail loudly rather than be discovered when a task is refused — and it currently cannot see the one file that is already over.

Related: #61 (the split that this pressure already forced).

issues.title: Swarm development bypasses the swarm: the repository's own changes are invisible to the ledger
issues.body:
The swarm's own repository is changed by work the swarm never issued, and the ledger cannot see any of it.

## What is verified

`main` carries two consecutive merges whose changes were authored by an operator-driven Claude Code session working directly against the repository, not by a controller-issued task:

- `a3e9537` (PR #56, closing #26)
- `206fce8` (PR #59, closing #57)

Neither has a task, an activation, a candidate the controller pinned, or a review in the ledger. Both were reviewed — by a manually-run Gemini chat, relayed by hand — and both reviews caught real defects. The ledger records none of it.

This is not the same problem as #58. #58 is about a review that happens outside the pipeline for work the controller *does* hold. This is about work the controller never held at all, where there is no `task_id` to attach anything to. A relayed-verdict route would not have recorded either of these merges.

## What is suspected, and the query that would settle it

206 commits on `main` carry a Claude Code session trailer, which suggests operator-driven sessions are how this repository has been developed for some time rather than an exception made twice this week. That is inference from commit trailers, not from the ledger, and it should not be treated as established.

The check is a ledger query on Tower: how many tasks have ever reached `COMPLETE` through `integration_completed` for the `agent-swarm` repository itself, and do their candidate SHAs appear in `main`'s history? If the answer is "few or none", the swarm has never meaningfully authored its own repository, and every guarantee this control plane provides has been applied to other repositories while its own development ran outside it.

## The decision this needs

Not a bug fix. A policy decision, made deliberately and written down:

**Option A — operator-driven changes are out-of-band by design.** Say so explicitly in the protocol and the deployment docs, and stop describing the ledger as a complete account of what reached `main`. Cheap, honest, and it means the swarm's own repository is permanently governed by something other than the swarm.

**Option B — swarm development runs through the swarm.** A change to this repository is a contract, authored by a worker under an activation, reviewed under an activation, integrated by the integrator. Expensive, slow for small fixes, and it has a bootstrapping problem: a change that breaks the controller cannot be landed by the controller.

**Option C — a declared boundary.** Certain classes of change (the controller itself, the hub, the supervisor) are operator-driven by policy and recorded as such through an explicit route, the way #26 records an out-of-band merge; everything else goes through the pipeline. This keeps the ledger honest about what it does not govern rather than silent about it.

## Why this matters more than it looks

The two changes those merges landed were about closing exactly this class of gap: something reaching a state with no event able to say how. The process that produced them has the same gap, one level up. A control plane whose own development is invisible to it can still be correct, but nobody can demonstrate that it is from the record it keeps.

Related: #58 (the relayed-verdict half of the same blindness).
issues.display_title: Swarm development bypasses the swarm: the repository's own changes are invisible to the ledger
